claims.text: Integrating experimental local-composition data with computational predictions in a machine-learning approach can enable fine control of magnetic ordering temperature in non-equiatomic HEAs.
The proposed machine-learning approach can enable fine control of the magnetocaloric response in non-equiatomic HEAs.
Targeted minor compositional changes and thermal processing can tune magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior.
Low-dimensional non-equiatomic HEAs exhibit local chemical and magnetic heterogeneities.
First-principles or spin-fluctuation calculations can provide temperature-dependent predictions relevant to magnetic behavior in transition-metal HEAs.

A machine-learning model correlating composition maps, annealing parameters, microstructure, and computational predictions can identify optimal minor compositional adjustments and processing conditions.
Surface and interface size effects are significant for the targeted low-dimensional samples.
Local chemical ordering and microstructural features mediate magnetic interactions at sub-microscopic length scales.
Machine learning can capture complex nonlinear relationships between processing variables and magnetic properties.
Machine-learning-directed adjustments can shift the magnetic phase-transition temperature.
Machine-learning-directed adjustments can enhance magnetic entropy change.
The magnetic ordering temperature and magnetocaloric-effect magnitude can be shifted either upward or downward in a controlled manner.
The proposed approach will optimize material performance relative to traditional trial-and-error methods.
Traditional coarse compositional adjustment and thermal processing provide insufficient precision for tuning magnetic interactions in non-equiatomic HEAs.
Uncaptured sub-microscopic heterogeneity can degrade the predictive accuracy of the machine-learning model.
Previous examples support improved tuning precision from the proposed data-driven approach.
